IntroText: Arabic nouns and adjectives can be definite or indefinite
VocabulariesText: The vocabulary that accompanies each lesson is intended to include all the words you need to understand the examples in the text of the lesson and to do the translation exercise that follows it. To make progress you will have to learn the vocabulary of each lesson as you come to it.
ExamplesText: All phrases used in each lesson are presented as appeared in the verses and highlighted in color to demonstrate their usage in the Qur’anic text.

IntroText:
Arabic has sound and broken plurals, with sound plurals considerably higher in Qur'an.

SOUND PLURALS
Word endings indicate masculine and feminine sound plurals, like house/houses and ox/oxen in English.

Arabic has nominative, accusative, and genitive cases.
  • Nominative is used for subject and predicates in non-verbal sentences.
  • Genitive denotes possession after prepositions.
  • Accusative is used when nominative or genitive cannot be used.

Lessons N0. 1 and Lesson No. 2 use nominatives, Lesson No. 4 introduce genitive, Lesson No. 8 introduce accusative.

FORM S OF DECLENSION
Declension types include five, with sub-divisions and special forms for feminine and masculine plural. Learning these types in tables helps structure knowledge.
Arabic prepositions take genitive case.
FIRST PERSON SINGULAR GENITIVE SUFFIX
Idafa, or 'annexation' represents the association of nouns with another, often indicating possession. It can also be a clause, as seen in the Qur'an, and can be a pronominal suffix or clause

Introduce accusative through verb, as direct object in most verbs. Arabic verbs are
trilateral with three radical roots, quadrilateral with four radicals. Verb has two
tenses: madi (past tense) and mudari (present tense). Sound verbs lack waw, ya,
and hamza radicals, have different forms and conjugations due to weak radicals or
doubled radicals. Common Qur'an verbs include قَالَqala and كَانَkana.
Qur'an contains 2,000 ma-related words, with frequent and important ones mentioned.
Qur'an hollow verbs, kana and qala, possess weak letters, effective learning.
Arabic has dual.
Practice and mental agility reveal less challenging with Arabic cardinal numbers.
Indo-European languages use prepositions and prefixes to create verb forms like 'admit', 'demit', 'emit', 'omit', 'permit','remit','submit', and 'transmit'.
Imperfect indicative emphasizes incompleteness of action, often translating into present or future meanings.
Interrogative particles ha and a- introduce questions, preceding wa- or fa-.
The subjunctive changes final short vowels to a and drops na if preceded by long vowels.

anna is an accusative particle, while إِنَّ inna is crucial.
inna lacks precise meaning.
inna and first person singular pronominal suffix create inni, inna-ni, and inna-na.
Jussive is a basic form of imperfect indicative, with a change in final vowel.
Here are the basic rules for the spelling of hamza.
Alladhi, an adjective, can be used as a pronoun like ma or man, but its adjectival use requires careful attention.
Elative in Arabic expresses comparative and superlative meanings.
Doubled verbs have identical second and third radicals, causing variations from sound verbs. Two rules cover these changes.
Lesson 10 briefly mentioned the exceptive particle ilia, which appears over 600 times in the Qur'an, and its usage rules need to be understood.
Hollow verbs have waw or ya as their middle radical and are divided into three distinct types.
The Qur'an typically introduces the vocative through the particle ya or the compound one ya ayyuha

The Qur'an provides examples of ordinals, fractions, and distributives, along with cardinal numbers, with limited distributives and general tables for each.
The Imperative is a second-person verb used for commands, not negatives. It originates from the second person of the Jussive, dropping the prefix ta- or tu-.
The Passive in Arabic is less common than the Active and is not used with agents in early Arabic. It uses different vowels and conjugation.
Lesson 7 explains that the second element of an idafa can be a clause, with temporal usage common. Qur'anic examples often use a verb, yawm or hin.
iyya- is a particle which is normally found only with the pronominal suffix iyya-ya to indicate the accusative.
Conditional sentences consist of a clause with a condition  اَلشَّرْط and a main clause with a response اَلْجَوَاب.
